note: The delivery-state section's own words: delivery states are terminal or non-terminal, and once a delivery reaches a terminal delivery state the state for that delivery will no longer change. The steps are received(0,0) unsettled, then the accepted outcome with settled set, then a further released state, which the third step's refusal pins. A terminal state is not just recorded and then overwritten: applying anything to it is refused with amqp:illegal-state, the shared condition whose definition is a peer sending what is not permitted in the current state. accepted also ends redelivery to this link, which the artifact's own text gives: at the source the accepted state means the message has been retired from the node. Its expectation is the accepted outcome's own rule, so the citation names it rather than only the sentence about state changes in general: a vector that expects a behaviour while citing a sentence one remove away is traced to the wrong clause.

The delivery-count is what makes a redelivery attempt countable, and the rejected outcome is the state that counts it: the type's text says the rejected outcome when applied to a message will cause the delivery-count to be incremented in the header of the rejected message. That sentence carries no RFC keyword and is not in the ledger as a clause id, so the citation is the type's captured statement and the rule is recorded here; the increment is asserted as an observable because a machine that recorded the state and not the count would be indistinguishable from one that did. Reading for the condition: this is an admitted step, so none is involved.

The clause is a MUST NOT and it is the counterpart of the rejected vector: the message is unchanged at the node, so the delivery-count of the header of the released message MUST NOT be incremented, and the same outcome is available for (re-)delivery to the same or other targets, which is what redelivery-allowed reports. Two vectors that differ only in the applied state are what separate a machine that increments on every terminal outcome from one that increments on rejected.

The accepted outcome does not increment the delivery-count, which is the third of the three outcomes whose counting rule differs and the one the ledger has no keyword-bearing statement for; the citation is the delivery-state section's terminal-state statement, and the rule is recorded here. The vector exists so that a machine incrementing on every terminal outcome fails on three vectors rather than one. Its expectation is the accepted outcome's own rule, so the citation names it rather than only the sentence about state changes in general: a vector that expects a behaviour while citing a sentence one remove away is traced to the wrong clause.

The one counting rule the artifact states with a keyword: if the delivery-failed flag is set, any messages modified MUST have their delivery-count incremented. The step applies modified with its first field true, so the count is 1; the modified outcome leaves the message available for redelivery, which is what separates it from rejected. Reading for the condition: an admitted step.

The artifact's second modified rule, also a keyword one: if undeliverable-here is set then any messages released MUST NOT be redelivered to the modifying link endpoint. The step carries null in delivery-failed and true in undeliverable-here, so the count stays 0 while redelivery-allowed turns false: the two fields of the same outcome move two different observables, and a machine that read one flag for both fails one of the two vectors.

received is the non-terminal state and it is not absorbing: a later received replaces the resume point, which is why the second step carries 1,5 and the expectation says so. Without section-number and section-offset as observables the second step would be indistinguishable from a no-op, and the two mandatory fields of received are exactly the ones the unkeyed statements describe: data and bytes prior to them cannot be retransmitted.

A non-terminal state followed by a terminal one: received(2,7) then rejected, which is the ordinary path a target takes when a message it has partly read turns out to be unprocessable. The delivery-count is 1 and the resume point is no longer reported, because the state is no longer received; a machine that kept the resume point after a terminal outcome would be reporting a resume point for a delivery that cannot be resumed.

The state codec is exercised through the machine: the applied state is a received whose body carries only section-number, so the mandatory section-offset is missing. The step is refused with amqp:decode-error and the delivery is left where it was, with its count unchanged, which is the harness law a refusal has to hold to: a refused step moves nothing. Reading for the condition: amqp:decode-error, as for the section codec.

A described value whose ulong descriptor is 255, which no declared type carries, applied as a delivery state. The delivery-state section defines a concrete set, so a state outside it is refused rather than recorded as an opaque value. Reading: amqp:decode-error.

A declared type that provides no delivery-state role, applied as a state: the header section, descriptor 112 with an empty list. The descriptor resolves and the type is a section, so this is the vector that pins the role rather than the descriptor table. Reading: amqp:decode-error.
